description: Team Skylize: Emir Özkan and Ata Özkan. We build AI systems and full-stack products. For Space Apps 2026 we built FlameSight by Skylize, a web dashboard that ranks NASA microgravity combustion findings by how closely they match any spacecraft or habitat atmosphere, with every number linked to its source.
summary:
FlameSight is a web dashboard that turns NASA’s microgravity combustion experiments into ranked, cited fire-safety evidence for any spacecraft or habitat atmosphere.

Fire behaves differently without gravity: flames go round and dim, spread in unfamiliar ways, and can keep burning below the oxygen levels that would stop them on Earth. Future Moon and Mars habitats are expected to run richer oxygen at lower pressure than the ISS. NASA has studied this for decades but the evidence is organized by experiment, not by the question a habitat designer actually asks.

In FlameSight, you pick an atmosphere (oxygen, pressure, airflow, material). It ranks 28 source-checked findings from 7 NASA investigations — BASS-II, Saffire I–VI, SoFIE-MIST, FLEX, ACME-BRE, CFI-G, SLICE — by how closely their test conditions match, labels the atmosphere Tested, Thin or Untested, and links every number to its source document and section.

Our key result: no flight test in the dataset matches the proposed 34% O₂ / 56.5 kPa exploration atmosphere. In the closest tests (Saffire VI), every sample burned and the flame spread.

FlameSight presents evidence, not verdicts. Gaps are results.
details:
Live app: https://www.flamesight.earth/ · Code: https://github.com/skylizeai-dev/skylize-nasa-space-apps-challenge

The problem

Fire behaves differently without gravity. With no buoyancy to carry hot gas away, flames become rounder and dimmer, spread in unfamiliar ways, and can keep burning below the oxygen levels that stop them on Earth. NASA has run flight experiments on this for more than a decade, aboard the ISS and in uncrewed Cygnus spacecraft. Future exploration habitats are expected to use richer-oxygen, lower-pressure atmospheres than the ISS. The engineers choosing those atmospheres and materials need one answer: what does NASA's evidence say about fire under these exact conditions, and how much evidence is there? Today that means reading dozens of papers and reports organized by experiment name. Crews far from Earth can't evacuate, so the gap matters.

What FlameSight by Skylize does

  1. Start from an atmosphere, not an experiment. A short setup asks where the fire would start (ISS cabin, exploration habitat, or custom), then oxygen (10–40%), pressure (30–110 kPa), airflow (0–50 cm/s) and the material type. An interactive 3D cabin illustration shows what the user is configuring. It is labeled "Illustration, not a simulation."
  2. See the evidence ranked. Findings are ordered by how closely their test conditions match the chosen atmosphere, weighted by how directly they bear on fire safety and by how complete their data is.
  3. Get a one-glance coverage verdict. Each atmosphere is labeled Tested, Thin or Untested, based on how many distinct test conditions lie nearby. Several readings from one burn count as one condition, so one experiment can't make a region look well tested.
  4. Check everything. Every evidence card shows what burned, under what conditions, what happened, and its score breakdown. A Verify drawer opens the source document and the exact section, slide or figure.
  5. See what's missing. An oxygen × pressure chart plots every tested condition by outcome, with the user's atmosphere as a crosshair. The gaps panel points to the nearest tested region, with one click to jump there.
  6. Read the implications. For the two preset atmospheres, 3–4 safety implications summarize the top evidence. Each one cites finding IDs and is labeled as AI-generated.
  7. Take it with you. Export the ranked findings as CSV.

What it shows for a Moon/Mars-type atmosphere (34% O₂, 56.5 kPa)

  • No flight test in the dataset matches it. The closest are Saffire VI burns at 28.8–31.0% O₂ and 54.1–55.2 kPa. In every one, the sample burned and the flame spread.
  • Thick plastic kept burning for a long time. A 1 cm PMMA slab burned for 780 s, and a 0.5 cm one-sided slab burned for 1,200 s.
  • Danger reached well beyond the flame. PMMA fires pushed cabin CO above the 24-hour crew limit and CO₂ above the 1-hour limit. Smoke was readily detected only at 981 s, after most of the hazardous gas had been released.
  • Oxygen level changes everything. In ACME-BRE, emulated-material flames self-extinguished within 40 s at 21% O₂, but burned steadily for minutes at 34% O₂.

Our conclusion is not "this atmosphere is unsafe." It is that we know the least about fire in the atmospheres we plan to use next. FlameSight makes that gap visible, and that tells researchers which test would add the most knowledge.

How it works

  • Dataset: 28 findings from 7 NASA investigations, stored as static JSON with a strict schema. Each finding records fuel, form, oxygen %, pressure (kPa), airflow (cm/s), flow direction, outcome, one plain-language sentence, safety relevance (1–3), source URL and source location.
  • Data rules: a missing value stays null and the card shows "not reported." Values are never guessed, interpolated or rounded. A finding appears only after every value has been checked against its cited source (source_checked). Independent human review is tracked separately and disclosed in docs/VERIFY.md. During the check, we removed or corrected values that came from the wrong statement, and we dropped two investigations (SPICE, SoFIE-GEL) that had no usable condition numbers.
  • Ranking (fully shown on the Method page): closeness = 1 − mean(|ΔO₂|/range, |ΔP|/range, |Δflow|/range), skipping unreported values score = closeness × (safety_relevance / 3) × completeness The same input always gives the same ranking. There is no black box and no AI in the ranking.
  • Works without AI. Ranking, coverage, chart, gaps and evidence are deterministic code. If the language model is unavailable, every core screen still works.
  • Accountable AI. AI text may only cite finding IDs that exist in the dataset, and it is always labeled "AI-generated from this dataset's NASA records."
  • Shareable state. The chosen atmosphere is stored in the URL, so anyone can reopen the exact view.

Who it helps

  • Habitat and mission designers choosing an atmosphere and materials.
  • Researchers deciding which condition to test next.
  • Students and the public exploring real NASA data without reading fifty papers.

What it is not

It is not a combustion simulator, a predictive model or a certified safety tool, and it is not a source of design limits. It is a way into NASA's evidence. FlameSight by Skylize is not affiliated with or endorsed by NASA.

What we hope to achieve

Next steps: full coverage of NASA's combustion investigations with continuous extraction; a material lookup (every condition a material was tested under); partner-agency data (ESA, JAXA, and others contributed to Saffire and ACME); and an "experiment planner" that ranks untested conditions by how much a new test would reduce uncertainty for planned missions. The same approach also fits NASA's fluids and materials science data.

Tools

Software (open source): Next.js (MIT), React (MIT), Tailwind CSS (MIT), three.js (MIT), Motion (MIT), Geist font (SIL OFL), TypeScript (Apache-2.0). Hosting: Vercel.
AI tools: Claude (Anthropic) was used as a coding assistant, to help draft finding rows (each value checked against its cited source), and to draft in-app summaries labeled “AI-generated” and used Skylize for govern the agents that we used to build this project. No AI-generated images. All visuals are code-drawn.
